st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Martínez accepts the cluster’s distinction between benchmark performance and real legal competence, and materially strengthens it by showing how comparison populations and essay-scoring methods can inflate apparent capability. st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between bounded task performance and general legal competence, and materially strengthens it by recalculating GPT-4’s bar-exam standing, identifying weaknesses in the competence proxy and essay grading, demonstrating prompt sensitivity, and linking overstated capability claims to unsafe reliance. It also develops the cluster’s governance case through a concrete demand for rigorous, transparent capability evaluation, though it says little about operating-model redesign.
qs: To the contrary, given the inevitable rapid growth of AI systems, the results of the present study underscore the importance of implementing rigorous and transparent evaluation measures to ensure that both the general public and relevant decisionmakers are made appropriately aware of the system’s capabilities, and to prevent these systems from being used in an unintentionally harmful or catastrophic manner.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between benchmark performance and dependable legal competence. It argues that success in a particular setting cannot establish general capability and that UBE percentiles are a weak proxy for practical lawyerly work; even accepting that proxy, GPT-4’s approximately 48th-percentile result among bar passers is materially more modest than earlier claims.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: Martínez supports the synthesis’s cautious distinction between benchmark performance and dependable legal competence. His lower estimates—especially for essay performance—and warning about unsafe reliance reinforce the view that current evidence supports limited, task-specific assistance more clearly than autonomous professional competence or safe self-representation.
qs: Moreover, when just looking at the essays, which more closely resemble the tasks of practicing lawyers and thus more plausibly reflect lawyerly competence, GPT-4’s performance falls in the bottom ∼15th percentile.

kp.k: The 90th-percentile claim lacks transparent methodological backing
kp.d: Martínez challenges OpenAI’s widely publicized claim that GPT-4 performed around the 90th percentile on the Uniform Bar Examination, rather than disputing that the model substantially improved over GPT-3.5. He finds that OpenAI’s technical report does not document its UBE percentile calculation and that the NCBE does not release official UBE percentiles. The paper distinguishes this reporting problem from the more transparent raw-score methodology in Katz et al. (2023).
qs: Although OpenAI details the methodology for computing most of its percentiles in A.5 of the Appendix of the technical report, there does not appear to be any such documentation for the methodology behind computing the UBE percentile.
Because there is no official percentile chart for UBE, all generally available online estimates are unofficial.

kp.k: Comparison populations substantially change GPT-4’s estimated ranking
kp.d: Approximate conversions from the February 2019 Illinois exam put a score of 300, slightly above GPT-4’s reported 298, at the 90th percentile. Martínez argues that February comparisons are skewed toward repeat takers who previously failed. July 2018 Illinois data instead place GPT-4 around the 68th percentile overall and 48th percentile on essays. These are approximate comparisons using Illinois examinations administered before the state adopted the UBE, not official national UBE percentile distributions.
qs: Indeed, examining the latest available percentile chart for the July exam estimates GPT-4’s UBE score to be ∼68th percentile, well below the 90th percentile figure cited by OpenAI (Illinois Board of Admissions to the Bar 2018).
Thus, the generally available Illinois percentile charts are based on pre-UBE Illinois bar exam data.

kp.k: First-time and passing-candidate comparisons yield lower estimated percentiles
kp.d: Using statistical estimates derived from NCBE data, the paper places GPT-4 at approximately the 62nd percentile overall, 79th percentile on multiple choice, and 42nd percentile on essays among first-time takers. For passing candidates, Section 3.2.2 and Tables 1 and 3 report approximately the 45th percentile overall, 69th on multiple choice, and 15th on essays. The abstract and discussion instead report approximately the 48th percentile overall for passing candidates; the document contains this numerical inconsistency. These comparisons are modeled exam-score rankings, not direct assessments of practicing attorneys.
qs: With regard to MBE, GPT-4 scored in the ∼79th percentile as compared to the ∼95th percentile February estimate and the 86th percentile July estimate.
With regard to the aggregate UBE score, GPT-4 scored in the ∼45th percentile.
The fourth main finding is that when examining only those who passed the exam, GPT-4’s performance is estimated to drop to ∼48th percentile overall, and ∼15th percentile on essays.

kp.k: Revised percentiles depend on consequential statistical assumptions
kp.d: The analysis assumes normally distributed scores, a first-time MBE mean of 143.8, an identical essay mean, and a combined UBE mean of 287.6. It estimates subsection standard deviations from July MBE distributions and the overall standard deviation using New York pass-rate and cutoff data. Passing-candidate comparisons exclude overall scores below 270 and, separately, subsection scores below 135. Martínez acknowledges that treating subsection failure as overall failure is implausible, while arguing that the resulting subsection biases would offset on average.
qs: Under the assumption that first-timers have approximately the same SD as that of the general test-taking population in July
To compute models’ performance on the individual components relative to qualified attorneys, a separate percentile was likewise computed after removing all subscores below 135.
Since scores on the two portions of the exam are likely to be highly but not directly correlated, this assumption is implausible.

kp.k: Multiple-choice performance replicates, unlike the disputed percentile interpretation
kp.d: Using official released NCBE questions, Martínez expands the original protocol from 18 to 50 trials: five repetitions across two prompts and five temperature settings, including additional settings of .25 and .7. Replication accuracy is 75.6% (95% CI: 74.7 to 76.4), versus 75.7% (95% CI: 74.2 to 77.1) in Katz et al. The study reports no significant replication-versus-original difference (p = .883), temperature effect (all relevant p values greater than .1), or difference between the two original prompt types (p = .741), supporting replication of the reported scaled MBE score of 158 under those methods.
qs: This brought the total temperature / prompt combinations to 10 as opposed to 6 in the original paper.
Second, GPT-4 was tested 5 times under each temperature / prompt combination as opposed to 3 times, bringing the total number of trials to 50 as opposed to 18.
Mean MBE accuracy across all trials in the replication here was 75.6% (95% CI: 74.7 to 76.4), whereas the mean accuracy across all trials in Katz et al. (2023) was 75.7% (95% CI: 74.2 to 77.1).

kp.k: More extensive prompting significantly improves multiple-choice performance
kp.d: A follow-up experiment compares minimally tailored basic prompting with a maximally tailored condition incorporating examples, answers, and explanations, using five trials per condition at temperature .5. Mean accuracy rises from 70.9% (95% CI: 68.1–73.7) to 79.5% (95% CI: 77.1–82.1), with p < .0001. Estimated scaled MBE scores are approximately 150 and 164 respectively. This is evidence of performance variation under the tested prompting configurations, not proof of equivalent improvements in real legal work.
qs: Mean MBE accuracy across all trials in the maximally tailored condition was descriptively higher at 79.5% (95% CI: 77.1–82.1), than in the minimally tailored condition at 70.9% (95% CI: 68.1–73.7).
As in the replication section, 5 trials were conducted for each of the two conditions.
Instead, both conditions featured the same temperature setting (.5).

kp.k: Essay grading weaknesses undermine precise capability claims
kp.d: Martínez questions the reported scaled essay score of 140 because Katz et al. do not report using formal grading rubrics or NCBE-trained graders and initially did not use blinded grading. Their comparisons relied on Maryland representative good answers with unspecified scores. Independent lawyers did subsequently grade blinded samples, but Martínez argues that this did not resolve the rubric, training, and calibration concerns. He does not establish a corrected essay score and acknowledges that the reported total of 298 is sufficiently above the common 270 passing threshold that substantial grading error would be needed to overturn the passage conclusion.
qs: Katz et al. (2023) do not report using an official or unofficial rubric of any kind, and instead simply describe comparing GPT-4’s answers to representative “good” answers from the state of Maryland.
the graders in Katz et al. (2023) (a subset of the authors who were trained lawyers) do not report expertise or training in bar exam grading.
it is true that the essay scores would have to have been wildly inaccurate in order to undermine the general conclusion of Katz et al. (2023) (i.e., that GPT-4 “passed the [uniform] bar exam”).

kp.k: Bar examination performance is an imperfect proxy for lawyering
kp.d: The author argues that UBE content is general rather than jurisdiction-specific, multiple-choice tasks differ from practicing lawyers’ work, and scores above the licensing threshold have limited professional incentives. He regards essay tasks as more representative of practice, making the relatively weak essay estimates particularly relevant to substitution claims. He also cautions that performance in one setting does not establish a model’s general ability or inability to perform a task.
qs: the tasks involved on the bar exam, particularly multiple-choice questions, do not reflect the tasks of practicing lawyers

obtaining a particularly high score or percentile past this threshold is less meaningful than for other exams (e.g. LSAT), where higher scores are taken into account for admission into select institutions (US News and World Report 2022).

some have pointed out that simply observing that GPT-4 underor overperforms at a task in some setting is not necessarily reliable evidence that it (or some other LLM) is capable or incapable of performing that task in general

kp.k: Overstated capabilities may encourage harmful legal reliance
kp.d: As prospective implications rather than measured outcomes, Martínez warns that publicity around the 90th-percentile claim may encourage judges, lawyers, and non-lawyers to delegate complex tasks that GPT-4 cannot adequately perform, potentially increasing legal misapplication, malpractice, ineffective self-representation, and unauthorized practice. Conversely, he suggests the relatively weak essay results might offer lawyers mild temporary reassurance about substitution, conditional on accepting the bar exam as a useful competence proxy.
qs: lawyers and non-lawyers may use GPT-4 for complex legal tasks for which it is incapable of adequately performing
the results might give practicing lawyers at least a mild temporary sense of relief regarding the security of the profession

plausibly increasing the rate of (a) misapplication of the law by judges; (b) professional malpractice by lawyers; and (c) ineffective pro se representation and/ or unauthorized practice of law by non-lawyers.

kp.k: Legal education and AI evaluation require stronger safeguards
kp.d: Martínez warns that students who overestimate GPT-4 may become less motivated to develop critical legal-analytical skills; this is a hypothesized educational risk, not an observed student outcome. He recommends prioritizing law-and-technology and law-and-AI instruction, alongside rigorous and transparent capability evaluations to inform public and professional decisions. He explicitly recognizes substantial progress from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 and anticipates further improvement, so his recommendations concern responsible evaluation and use rather than a claim that present limitations will persist.
qs: particularly if under the impression that GPT-4’s level of mastery of those skills already surpasses that to which a typical law student could be expected to reach.

The results also indicate that law schools and the legal profession should prioritize instruction in areas such as law and technology and law and AI, which, despite their importance, are currently not viewed as descriptively or normatively central to the legal academy (Martínez and Tobia 2023).

the results of the present study underscore the importance of implementing rigorous and transparent evaluation measures to ensure that both the general public and relevant decisionmakers are made appropriately aware of the system’s capabilities

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Martínez argues that GPT-4’s bar-exam performance provides substantially weaker grounds for assuming lawyer-level competence or imminent lawyer substitution than the publicised 90th-percentile claim suggests.
pts.d: The author estimates GPT-4 at approximately the 68th percentile against July examinees and the 62nd percentile against first-time examinees, with essay performance at approximately the 48th and 42nd percentiles respectively. Against passing examinees, the results section and Tables 1 and 3 report approximately the 45th percentile overall, whereas the abstract and discussion report approximately the 48th; both report approximately the 15th percentile on essays. Martínez conditionally infers a limited, temporary reassurance about professional security because essays more closely resemble lawyers’ work. This is an inference from benchmark performance, not an observed finding about employment or actual legal-service delivery.

pts.k: Martínez predicts that overstated capability claims could encourage inappropriate reliance on GPT-4 for complex legal tasks and thereby worsen legal outcomes.
pts.d: The proposed mechanism is that extensive publicity about superior bar-exam performance leads lawyers and non-lawyers to entrust tasks to GPT-4 that it cannot adequately perform. The author identifies possible judicial misapplication of law, lawyer malpractice, ineffective self-representation and unauthorised practice by non-lawyers. These are prospective risks rather than harms measured by the study.

pts.k: Martínez warns that exaggerated perceptions of GPT-4’s competence could discourage students from developing legal-analysis skills, and recommends greater emphasis on law-and-AI education.
pts.d: The educational risk depends on students believing that GPT-4 already exceeds the legal-analytical mastery they could reasonably attain. The paper does not measure student motivation or educational outcomes. Its recommendation is that law schools and the profession prioritise instruction in law and technology and law and AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a statistical re-estimation of exam percentiles, an MBE replication, a prompting experiment and a methodological review of essay grading—not a study of practising lawyers’ work.
pts.d: Martínez compares July 2018 and February 2019 pre-UBE Illinois conversion charts and constructs first-time-examinee distributions using official NCBE information and New York pass-rate and cutoff data. The MBE replication yields 75.6% mean accuracy versus 75.7% in Katz et al., with no significant difference between studies and no significant temperature effect. A separate experiment finds 79.5% accuracy with maximally tailored prompting versus 70.9% with minimally tailored prompting, a statistically significant difference. The essay critique concerns the absence of a reported formal rubric, NCBE grader training and fully comparable blinding and calibration procedures. The paper does not establish a corrected essay score through independent official regrading. Claims about professional displacement, harmful reliance and student apathy are implications drawn from these findings, not directly tested outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The conclusions concern GPT-4’s launch-era capabilities and are conditional on the validity of the bar exam as a proxy for legal competence; no timetable for lawyer replacement is offered.
pts.d: Published online on 30 March 2024, the paper re-evaluates claims accompanying GPT-4’s March 2023 launch. The percentile calculations initially assume the reported total score of 298 is valid, use normal-distribution and scaling assumptions, and define the passing comparison using a total cutoff of 270. Subsection comparisons use cutoffs of 135, with the author acknowledging the implausibility of assuming that everyone failing a subsection failed overall. The paper stresses that general legal doctrine and multiple-choice tasks differ from practice and that performance in one setting does not establish general capability or incapability. Its professional-security implication is expressly temporary. Martínez anticipates substantial future improvement but provides no date or quantified displacement forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The identified stakeholders are practising lawyers, judges, clients, self-represented individuals, law students, educators, AI developers and public decision-makers.
pts.d: Practising lawyers may reassess both substitution risks and the appropriateness of relying on AI. Judges, clients and self-represented individuals face the hypothesised consequences of incorrect legal work. Students may underinvest in analytical skills, while law schools and the profession are urged to strengthen technology-related instruction. Developers are urged to provide rigorous, transparent capability evaluations so that users and decision-makers can make informed choices. The paper does not distinguish effects by law-firm size, legal-market segment or pricing model.
